posts.title: Blocking the first felt of autumn
posts.excerpt: The steamer came back on last Wednesday after the straw season. A note on the first felt hood of the autumn.
posts.content:
The steamer came back on last Wednesday after the straw season. A note on the first felt hood of the autumn.

Waking the blocks

After a summer of straw, the wooden blocks are wiped down and rubbed with a little wax before any felt goes near them.

The first hood is always a soft wool in charcoal, because it forgives a cold hand.

A crown in one pull

Steamed until it relaxes, the felt is drawn down over the block in a single, even pull and pinned at the band line.

By evening it had dried into shape, and the season had begun.

Felt remembers the hand that shaped it, so the hand has to be patient.

Rin Tsubaki

posts.title: Why we still block by hand
posts.excerpt: A press could do it faster. We still shape every crown over a wooden block, by hand. Here is why.
posts.content:
A press could do it faster. We still shape every crown over a wooden block, by hand. Here is why.

On the block

Blocking sets the line of a hat: the height of the crown, the tilt of the brim, the small curve where they meet.

On wood you can feel it happen: the felt warms, gives a little, then begins to hold the edge of your thumb.

What the hand learns

Each material behaves differently. Fur felt is stubborn; straw goes brittle in a dry room.

Working by hand keeps us close enough to notice, hat by hat.

The block is the oldest tool in the atelier, and still the most honest.

Rin Tsubaki

posts.title: Straw season at the bench
posts.excerpt: From late spring the felt is put away and the straw comes out. What changes on the bench when the weather warms.
posts.content:
From late spring the felt is put away and the straw comes out. What changes on the bench when the weather warms.

Damp, not wet

Straw is sized and dampened just enough to bend; too much water and the weave loosens and loses its shine.

We block boaters and sun hats in the morning, while the air is still cool and slow to dry.

Lighter hands

A straw brim is wired at the edge and bound with a fine ribbon, so it keeps its line in a summer wind.

There is no rushing straw, but there is a gentle rhythm to it.

A summer hat should feel like shade you can carry.

Rin Tsubaki

posts.title: How to measure your head
posts.excerpt: A hat that fits sits quietly and stays put. A short guide to measuring at home with a soft tape.
posts.content:
A hat that fits sits quietly and stays put. A short guide to measuring at home with a soft tape.

Where the band sits

Run the tape round your head about a finger's width above the eyebrows and ears, where the hat band will rest.

Keep it snug but not tight, and read the number at the back where the two ends meet.

Between sizes

If you fall between two sizes, choose the larger: a thin ribbon inside the band takes up the difference.

Write the number down and bring it to a fitting, or simply add it to your order.

A good fit is something you stop noticing after the first minute.

Rin Tsubaki

posts.title: Caring for a felt brim
posts.excerpt: A felt hat can last for decades. A few quiet habits that keep a brim in shape through the wet months.
posts.content:
A felt hat can last for decades. A few quiet habits that keep a brim in shape through the wet months.

Rain and steam

If the brim is caught in the rain, shake it off and let it dry upside down on its crown, away from heat.

A little steam from a kettle relaxes a bent edge; shape it with your fingers and let it cool.

Storing it

Keep a felt hat in its box or resting on its crown, never flat on its brim.

Brush it now and then with a soft brush, always in the direction of the nap.

A hat that is looked after slowly takes on the shape of its wearer.

Rin Tsubaki

posts.title: A day of fittings
posts.excerpt: Saturdays are kept for fittings. A short account of one day at the atelier, from opening to the last hat box.
posts.content:
Saturdays are kept for fittings. A short account of one day at the atelier, from opening to the last hat box.

Eleven o'clock

The door opens, the mirror is wiped down, and the first visitor tries three crowns before saying a word.

We measure, then watch how the hat is worn, because the tilt matters as much as the size.

Late afternoon

Ribbons are chosen, bands are pinned, and a made-to-order cloche begins on the block.

By closing, two hats are boxed in tissue, ready to be collected the following week.

Every head is different. That is the whole pleasure of the work.

Rin Tsubaki
